Count Basie. The American pianist and bandleader whose orchestra became one of the defining engines of the swing era, and whose impeccable sense of rhythm and minimalist piano touch led one of jazz's greatest ensembles.

He started as a vaudeville performer and pianist in the nineteen-twenties, and formed his famous orchestra in nineteen thirty-five in Kansas City. Basie was famous for his economy on the piano. Rather than playing elaborate passages, he played spare, perfectly-timed chords. Rhythm was his instrument.

He led one of the greatest big bands, the All-American Rhythm Section, featuring legendary soloists like Lester Young on tenor saxophone and Buck Clayton on trumpet. Recordings like One O'Clock Jump and April in Paris became jazz standards, and his blues feel was instantly recognizable. He competed directly with Duke Ellington for prestige, though he offered a leaner, swinging alternative to Ellington's lush orchestration.

Basie toured extensively, bringing swing to millions. He was more commercially successful than many contemporaries, yet never lost critical respect. The band continued performing into the nineteen-eighties. Basie remained one of jazz's most durable and consistent figures, and his influence on rhythm-section playing remains unmatched in jazz history. He shares this legacy with the jazz tradition itself, and with his great rival Duke Ellington, and with his contemporary peer Louis Armstrong.
